entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses AI/ML, computational modeling, high-throughput molecular profiling and experiments to study how tumours evolve, with the aim of improving cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment. Current projects include early cancer evolution (for example Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia, using organoid models and multiomic profiling) and tissue ecology in ER+ breast cancer. A large part of the work is single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and spatial multiomics, including how cancer cells and the microenvironment coevolve. The lab also does computational pathology and builds prognostic biomarkers from genomic and imaging data. Evolutionary and mathematical modelling of tumour growth is also part of the group's approach.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, computational/ML methods and single-cell and spatial omics in cancer. Less emphasis on WGS and structural-variant calling, and a US move would need a visa.

flags: PI is still at Stanford; no move found.

The Stanford School of Medicine team page (med.stanford.edu/curtislab/team.html) could not be opened (certificate error). Members come from curtis-lab.com/people, which does not date its content or say whether students are PhD candidates. The two pages may differ.

Search snippets of the Stanford team page showed a different, possibly older roster (e.g. Kathleen Houlahan, Ryan Schenck, Noah Greenwald, Katherine Liu). I did not confirm whether they are still in the lab and did not include them.
Stanford Profiles (via search snippet) also listed postdoc sponsorships for Nicola Calonaci, Yufeng He and Seongyeol Park. Calonaci and He are not on curtis-lab.com, so their status is unverified.
Clinical fellows (Marni McClure, Audris Chiang, Colin Bergstrom, Zach Ziheng Xu), a medical student and a post-bacc were excluded.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI/ML models for functional genomics. These include interpretable neural networks of DNA and RNA regulation, and large language and foundation models for chemistry and genomics. It studies cancer evolution and tumour-environment interactions, including how cancer cells reprogram gene expression. A central example is orphan non-coding RNAs (oncRNAs), which are largely absent from normal tissue and promote metastasis. It also studies post-transcriptional regulation in cancer and neurodegeneration, for example tRNA fragments (tiRNAs) that suppress breast cancer metastasis. Its methods pair unbiased experimental screens with computational analysis.

fit.reason: Strong overlap on computational and ML methods for genomics and on cancer transcriptomics, but the lab centres on RNA biology and model building rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Google DeepMind
entries.focus: DeepMind's science teams build AI models for biology, and AlphaFold is the best known. AlphaFold predicts protein structures and, in later versions, complexes with other biomolecules. AlphaGenome is a sequence-to-function model that predicts regulatory effects of DNA variants, including non-coding variants. It matched or beat other leading tools on 25 of 26 variant-effect tests. It was published in Nature, with model weights released and free noncommercial access. A September 2026 report says there is also an 'AlphaGenome Atlas' browser for mapping human genetic variation, which I did not verify against an official source.

fit.reason: AlphaGenome's non-coding and somatic variant-effect prediction and its ML methods for genomics overlap with the student's cancer genomics and computational interests. entries.name: Tempus AI
entries.focus: Tempus is a precision-medicine and AI company that runs clinical-grade next-generation sequencing for cancer patients. The assays cover DNA and RNA, including tumour/normal and whole-exome or transcriptome profiling. It links the molecular data to de-identified clinical records, and uses that large multimodal dataset to train machine-learning models. These models support treatment matching, clinical-trial matching and biomarker discovery. It also licenses the data to pharma partners for drug development. The intern project I found in the 2026 summer posting was a somatic copy number model of the cancer genome, which fits its genomics-focused research work. I could not load the official team pages to confirm further detail on the research groups.

fit.reason: Its work centres on tumour sequencing, somatic variant and copy-number analysis, and ML on genomics, and there is a PhD bioinformatics internship. The costs are that it is US-based (Chicago, needs a visa), it requires graduation within about a year, and it has little single-cell or spatial emphasis.

flags: I could not load Tempus's official careers or team pages (a 429 error). Program details come from job-board mirrors (Revolution, Lightbank, Simplify), so confirm them on Tempus's careers site.
I found no PhD fellowship, residency, student researcher or visiting programs.
The leads' backgrounds are partly unverified. I found no named head of a computational biology or AI-for-science team, so the three leads are company executives.
The 2026 internship asked for graduation within about a year, which excludes a first-year PhD student. The Translational Research and Scientific Solutions postings were not read in full.
The student would likely need US work authorization for these roles.

entries.name: Noetik
entries.focus: Noetik is an AI-native biotech, founded in 2022, that builds machine-learning models for cancer therapeutics. It generates large multimodal tumour datasets, with a focus on spatial biology (genomics, transcriptomics and proteomics). It trains self-supervised foundation models of patient tumour and tissue biology on this data. Its internal 'Data Foundry' is a lab-in-the-loop platform for large-scale spatial data. Its Therapeutics group uses the models for target discovery, patient stratification and diagnostics in oncology and immunotherapy. A 2023 seed round of $14M was led by DCVC; I did not check for later funding.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in ML for cancer, spatial and single-cell omics and transcriptomics, but there is no student program, the company is US-based, and the work centres on spatial multimodal data rather than WGS or structural variants.

flags: No internship, fellowship, residency or student researcher programme was found on the Noetik careers page. It only offers 'Express interest' forms (via Greenhouse) for four areas: Artificial Intelligence, Engineering, Data Foundry and Therapeutics.
I could not see any individual job postings, so I could not check requirements, locations or deadlines.
Working in the US would likely need a visa for a Canadian student.
A cold outreach or general expression of interest to the AI research team is the realistic route; ask about a short-term or research-collaboration role.
